questions.prompt: A Navigation 3 `NavDisplay` uses only `rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator()`. Two `Detail(id)` entries on the back stack each call `viewModel<DetailViewModel>()`. What happens?

choices.text: Each entry gets its own instance, cleared as soon as that entry is popped
Both get one shared instance, scoped to the Activity, not each entry
Each entry gets its own instance, but none is cleared until exit
It fails to compile until a ViewModel decorator is in the list

questions.explanation: Without `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator`, a ViewModel is scoped to the nearest `ViewModelStoreOwner`, usually the Activity, so both entries get the same instance and it outlives them. Adding that decorator (from `lifecycle-viewmodel-navigation3`) gives each entry its own `ViewModelStoreOwner`: the ViewModel is created when the entry is added and cleared when it is removed.

sources.title: Save and manage navigation state
sources.claim: By default ViewModels are scoped to the nearest ViewModelStoreOwner, typically the Activity or Fragment; `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator` provides a ViewModelStoreOwner per NavEntry so a ViewModel is created when the entry is added and cleared when it is removed.

questions.prompt: Your team's SDK adds a `streamUploads()` API whose shape may still change. With Kotlin's opt-in mechanism, how do you make callers acknowledge that?

choices.text: Mark it `@Deprecated(level = WARNING)` until the API is final
Mark it `@OptIn`, so callers get a warning whenever they use it
Mark it with your own annotation class marked `@RequiresOptIn`
Make it `internal` and expose it to callers with `@PublishedApi`

questions.explanation: The library author declares a marker annotation class annotated with `@RequiresOptIn` and puts that marker on the unstable API. Callers then opt in with `@OptIn(Marker::class)`, by propagating the marker, or module-wide. `@OptIn` is the caller's side, and `@Deprecated` says the opposite of "new but unstable".

sources.title: Opt-in requirements
sources.claim: Library authors create an opt-in requirement annotation by annotating an annotation class with `@RequiresOptIn` and mark API elements with it; clients opt in with `@OptIn`, by propagating the annotation, or at file or module level.

questions.prompt: Your news feed prefetches full-resolution images and autoplay video ahead of the scroll. How should it adapt to the user's network, and how do you detect the network's properties on Android?

model_answer.summary: Prefetch less, or at lower quality, on metered networks, deciding meteredness from `NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED` rather than from Wi-Fi vs cellular, and react to changes with a network callback.
key_points: Check `NetworkCapabilities.hasCapability(NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED)` to decide whether data costs the user, and cut prefetching or quality when it is metered
Don't infer meteredness or bandwidth from the transport: Wi-Fi isn't always unmetered or faster than mobile
Use `getLinkDownstreamBandwidthKbps()` as the bandwidth estimate for choosing image or video quality
Register a default `NetworkCallback` and adapt in `onCapabilitiesChanged` when the network changes

questions.explanation: The tempting answer is "only prefetch on Wi-Fi", but the Android docs call the transport a poor proxy: a phone hotspot is Wi-Fi and metered. The capability check and bandwidth estimate describe the network itself, and the callback keeps the feed right when the user walks out of range.

sources.title: Read network state
sources.claim: A network with NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED doesn't bill the user for data; hasTransport is a poor proxy for bandwidth or meteredness, so use getLinkDownstreamBandwidthKbps() and hasCapability(NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED); listen for changes with a default NetworkCallback's onCapabilitiesChanged.

questions.prompt: In a Navigation 3 app, how do you give each screen on the back stack its own ViewModel, and when is that ViewModel created and cleared?

model_answer.summary: Add `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator()` to `NavDisplay`'s `entryDecorators`, so `viewModel()` inside an entry is scoped to that entry: created when it is added to the back stack and cleared when it is removed.
key_points: By default a ViewModel is scoped to the nearest `ViewModelStoreOwner`, usually the Activity or Fragment, not to a screen
A ViewModel created with `viewModel()` inside an entry's content is then scoped to that entry's key
It is created when the entry is added to the back stack and cleared when the entry is removed

questions.explanation: In Navigation 3 you own the back stack, and ViewModel scoping is opt-in through an entry decorator. Forgetting it is a common bug: every screen of one type shares an Activity-scoped ViewModel that never clears.

sources.title: Save and manage navigation state
sources.claim: ViewModels default to the nearest ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity or Fragment); the `lifecycle-viewmodel-navigation3` decorator `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator`, added to entryDecorators after the saveable state holder decorator, scopes `viewModel()` to the NavEntry's key, created when added and cleared when removed.

questions.prompt: A library's marker annotation is declared `@RequiresOptIn` with no `level`. A client calls a function marked with it without opting in. What happens?

choices.text: A compiler warning only, since opt-in is advisory by default
A crash at runtime the first time that function is called
Nothing, unless the module turns on `-opt-in` for the marker
A compile error, since the default opt-in level is `ERROR`

questions.explanation: `RequiresOptIn.Level` is `ERROR` by default, which makes opting in mandatory; the author must choose `WARNING` for advisory opt-in. It is checked at compile time, and the module-wide `-opt-in` option is one way to opt in, not a switch that turns checking on.

sources.title: Opt-in requirements
sources.claim: An opt-in requirement level is ERROR (mandatory, the default) or WARNING (advisory); clients can opt in locally with @OptIn, per file, or module-wide with the -opt-in compiler option.

questions.prompt: Your app downloads HD video previews only when `hasTransport(TRANSPORT_WIFI)` is true. What does the Android documentation say about this check?

choices.text: It's correct, since Wi-Fi networks never bill users for data
It's a poor proxy; check `NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED` instead
It's fine, as long as `TRANSPORT_ETHERNET` is also allowed
It's correct, once the user has granted the Wi-Fi state permission

questions.explanation: The docs say the transport is a poor proxy for bandwidth or meteredness: an app can't assume Wi-Fi is always unmetered or faster than mobile. Use `hasCapability(NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED)` for cost and `getLinkDownstreamBandwidthKbps()` for bandwidth.

sources.title: Read network state
sources.claim: Querying hasTransport is a poor proxy for the bandwidth or meteredness of the network; apps can't assume Wi-Fi is always unmetered and should use hasCapability with NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED.
